What are the observations of the essayist on books in the passage?
context: In proportion as a book is more loosely constructed, the paragraphs tend to become more diffuse. You often have to search through all the paragraphs of a chapter to find the sentences you can construct into a statement of a single argument. Some books make you search in vain, and some do not even encourage the search. A good book usually summarizes itself as its arguments develop. If the author summarizes his arguments for you at the end of a chapter, or at the end of an elaborate section, you should be able to look back over the preceding pages and find the materials he has brought together in the summary. In The Origin of Species, Darwin summarizes his whole argument for the reader in a last chapter, entitled “Recapitulation and Conclusion.” The passage then discusses omitted steps in arguments, the reader’s duty to identify arguments, the distinction between inductive and deductive reasoning, assumptions and self-evident propositions, and tautologies.

question: Make a precis of the prescribed passage in about one-third of its length, in your own words, without giving a title.
context: Every individual soul is an undeveloped entity, capable of transforming animal instincts through discipline and spiritual growth. Human progress becomes conscious and deliberate; individuals can transform themselves and thereby contribute to transforming the world. Each person is unique and must find a centre that unifies their nature through reflection and meditation. Moral life requires meaningful action, respect for the dignity of others, social harmony and self-sacrifice. The passage concludes that moral progress requires acceptance of one’s given nature combined with the adventure of building higher, with the aim not merely to maintain life but to elevate it.
